title: "Rebase Conflicts"
---

# Rebase Conflicts: How They Differ from Merge Conflicts

After this page you can finish a conflicted rebase one commit at a time.

## One commit at a time

A merge conflict happens **once**, at the join. A rebase conflict happens **each time** a copied commit does not apply onto the new parent.

```text
 merge: one fight at M

 A ← B ← C ← M
      ↑      ↑
      D ← E

 rebase: a fight at D', then maybe again at E'

 A ← B ← C ← G ← D'  ←  E'
                 ▲ stop    ▲ stop
```

Markers look the same (`<<<<<<<`). `git status` during a rebase says `rebase in progress` and names the commit being applied.

```bash
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/ping.py
git status
```

## The loop

1. Edit files, remove markers.
2. `git add` the resolved paths.
3. `git rebase --continue` (not `git commit`, unless Git asks you to).
4. Repeat until Git prints `Successfully rebased`.

```bash
nvim src/ping.py
git add src/ping.py
git rebase --continue
```

If the commit becomes empty (your patch is already in the new base):

```bash
git rebase --skip
```

Give up:

```bash
git rebase --abort
```

## Ours / theirs are swapped from merge

During **merge**, `--ours` is the branch you had checked out (`main`). During **rebase**, you checked out the feature and Git replays onto `main`: `--ours` is the **upstream** (the new base), `--theirs` is the commit being replayed.

That swap surprises everyone once. Prefer reading the markers over `--ours` until it is boring.

## `rerere`

With `rerere.enabled` (chapter 2), Git records the resolution. A later rebase that hits the same hunk applies it again. On a long-lived feature branch that rebases onto `main` daily, this is the difference between pain and a two-second continue.

## After success

```bash
git log --oneline --graph --decorate main feat/ping-json
```

A straight line from `main` through your copied commits. Then `git switch main && git merge --ff-only feat/ping-json`.
